subject: operating-systems
title: Files and file metadata
summary: A file system names persistent data, records metadata, and maps logical file offsets to storage blocks.

questions.prompt: Which item is file metadata rather than file content?
questions.answerKey: Permissions are metadata describing access to the file.
questions.explanation: Size, owner, timestamps, and block pointers are other metadata examples.

questions.prompt: Why does a file descriptor usually identify an open-file entry rather than just a path string?
options: It carries per-open state such as current offset and access mode
It stores the entire file in a register
questions.answerKey: An open-file description can track offset, flags, and references to the underlying file object.
questions.explanation: Path lookup and open-file state are distinct abstractions.

questions.prompt: A file is opened with append semantics. Where should each write be placed?
options: At the end of the file as defined by the append operation
questions.answerKey: Append writes are positioned at the end for each write according to the OS semantics.
questions.explanation: Concurrent append behavior depends on the filesystem and API guarantees.

questions.prompt: Why can sequential access outperform random access on a disk-backed file?
options: It reduces seek/positioning overhead and benefits from read-ahead
It always uses less logical data
questions.answerKey: Adjacent or predicted blocks can be read efficiently and with fewer positioning costs.
questions.explanation: The gap depends on storage technology and cache state.

questions.prompt: Distinguish a file name, an open file descriptor, and the underlying file object.
questions.answerKey: A name is a directory entry used to locate a file. An open file descriptor is a per-process handle referring to an open-file description with flags and offset. The underlying file object holds persistent metadata and data-block mappings and may have multiple names or descriptors.
questions.explanation: The exact object names differ across operating systems, but the layers are distinct.

questions.prompt: Explain why flushing a user-space buffer is not always the same as durable storage.
questions.answerKey: Flushing a library buffer may only issue data to the kernel. The kernel and storage device can still cache writes, so an explicit synchronization operation and device-specific guarantees may be needed before claiming persistence after a crash.

rubric.criterion: Distinguishes user buffer from kernel/device cache

questions.explanation: Durability is a storage-stack property, not just a language-library flush.
